title: Knowledge Graph Population from News Streams
domain: Online multilingual news streams aggregated into same-event article clusters; individual article text and semi-structured metadata, optionally associated images, video/audio transcripts, and OCR text.
research_problem: How to generate a dynamic, high-quality knowledge graph that updates with world changes by extracting entities, relations, events, and novel facts from unstructured, multilingual news streams. The application setting is media-content indexing, search, event exploration, and KG maintenance, where static encyclopedic KGs omit emerging entities and current facts.
methodology: The end-to-end workflow is: (1) crawl RSS feeds and parse article text/images; (2) represent articles with NER/POS-derived entities, nouns, and noun chunks, weighted with modified TF-IDF and time; (3) use k-NN tracking and DBSCAN detection to aggregate same-story news; (4) obtain semantic entities through multimodal entity linking, including spaCy NER/POS, visual recognition, OCR, and speech-to-text inputs; (5) dynamically create provisional person 'aspirants' from repeated NIL mentions, then have humans accept, merge as aliases, or reject them; (6) create candidate entity pairs in sentences and use fine-tuned BERT with entity/type markers to classify ontology relations; (7) merge duplicate triples and validate RDF graphs with ontology-derived SHACL type/cardinality/disjoint constraints, exploiting redundancy across an event; (8) aggregate unique triples across events, classify their correctness from 18 redundancy/prediction features, and ingest threshold-passing triples into VKG. Separately, VLX-Stories represents events in an event ontology using who/what/where/when/topic properties.
pipeline_stages: ["Text preprocessing", "Entity and concept extraction", "Entity typing", "Entity resolution and linking", "Relation and triple extraction", "Event extraction", "Graph construction", "Knowledge fusion and deduplication", "Graph validation and correction", "Graph updating"]
entity_extraction: ["Entity and concept extraction", "Entity typing", "Entity resolution and linking"]
ontology_schema_use: VKG is an encyclopedic KG merged from Freebase, Wikidata, and Wikipedia. It supplies entity candidates, an ontology of relation predicates and entity types, and SHACL constraints. The system also defines a VLX-Event Ontology, inspired by journalism's who/what/where/when questions plus topic, category, semantic-pattern entities, and article context. The schema constrains RE outputs and RDF validation.

title: Semi-supervised Generative Open Information Extraction
domain: English unstructured natural-language sentences; training additionally uses a prompted sentence plus a candidate tree-form extraction for the verification task.
research_problem: Improve generative OpenIE when high-quality labelled training data are scarce and bootstrapped labels are noisy or unsuitable for differing application-specific annotation preferences. The objective is to exploit unlabeled Wikipedia text while filtering unreliable pseudo-extractions.
methodology: The proposed Semi-supervised UIE-OIE is a T5-small-based generative OpenIE system. It first jointly pre-trains extraction and pseudo-label-verification tasks using task prompts. Extraction maps a sentence directly to a UIE-inspired tree sequence in which each predicate is a relation node with subject/object argument leaves; no schema sequence is supplied because OpenIE is schema-free. Verification maps a sentence plus one tree-form extraction to true/false. Negative verification examples are synthesized by mismatching subject–predicate pairs across tuples, swapping subject and object, and extending an object with remaining sentence text. In semi-supervised training, identically initialized student and EMA mean-teacher models are used. For unlabeled sentences, the teacher greedily generates trees; malformed outputs are removed, candidates are filtered by a perplexity threshold, and each extraction is verified. The student trains on gold labels plus retained pseudo-labels with supervised, consistency, and R-Drop symmetric-KL regularization losses; the teacher is updated by EMA. Verification and extraction examples are balanced by random sampling.

title: Named Entity Extraction for Knowledge Graphs: A Literature Overview
domain: Unstructured natural-language text, including documents and shorter/noisy text such as tweets, micro-posts, SMS texts, and chats, as discussed across reviewed studies.
research_problem: The paper addresses how named entities in unstructured natural-language text can be recognized, disambiguated, and linked to knowledge-base resources as a central part of lifting text into computer-processable knowledge graphs. Its objective is to consolidate advances from 2014–2019, organize NER/NED/NEL methods and their sub-tasks, summarize datasets, tools, and reported comparative results, and identify evaluation and research gaps.
methodology: This is a literature overview, not a new executable Text-to-KG system, so no single methodology family, system type, or supervision setting is applicable. The authors searched ACM, IEEE, ScienceDirect, Springer, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for sufficiently high-quality, in-scope 2014–2019 papers on at least one of NER, NED, and NEL; they screened 362 abstracts down to 89 core papers, categorized them by task, and added a few papers through snowballing. The review presents the operational sequence from preprocessing through NER, NED, and NEL: NER identifies mention spans; NED resolves the intended entity; NEL assigns a KB/LOD IRI. It classifies NER as rule/knowledge-based, learning-based, and feature-inferring neural approaches; NED as traditional independent/collective and neural approaches; and NEL as independent/feature-engineering, collective, and neural approaches, also distinguishing disambiguation-only from end-to-end/joint methods. Its detailed contributions are: (1) an integrated NER–NED–NEL framing of named-entity extraction for KG lifting; (2) diagrams of the NL-to-KG workflow and NEL sub-tasks; (3) consolidated comparisons of reported NEL results, datasets, KB targets, and tools; (4) a synthesis of trends toward joint and end-to-end context-aware neural methods; and (5) a research agenda covering NER integration, multilinguality, domain transfer, NIL entities, and comparable KG-oriented evaluation.

The review does not introduce or learn a new ontology/schema.

title: KGen: a knowledge graph generator from biomedical scientific literature
domain: Unstructured biomedical scientific literature in natural-language text form, specifically scientific-paper abstracts and their conclusion subsections in the evaluation.
research_problem: The paper addresses automated or semi-automated construction of ontology-linked knowledge graphs from unstructured biomedical scientific literature. The challenge is to identify biomedical entities and explicit or implicit relations in long, complex sentences containing abbreviations, coreferences, and domain-specific terminology, then represent the extracted knowledge as RDF triples and link it to biomedical ontologies.
methodology: KGen is a modular four-step pipeline. First, preprocessing tokenizes and splits text into sentences, resolves coreferences and abbreviations, and simplifies long sentences. Second, semantic role labeling extracts main subject-predicate-object relations, while dependency parsing and rule-based transformations extract secondary relations involving compounds, modifiers, and noun structures. Third, biomedical named entities and lemmatized verbs are mapped to UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers, and SPARQL queries retrieve corresponding classes, properties, or attributes in a selected BioPortal ontology. Fourth, extracted triples are enriched with local URIs, rdfs:label links, and owl:sameAs mappings, then serialized in Turtle; Graphviz can optionally visualize the graph. Human experts may inspect or modify intermediate artifacts in the semi-automatic workflow.

ScispaCy identifies biomedical entities and UMLS CUIs; lemmatized verbs are also mapped. SPARQL queries to the NCBO BioPortal endpoint retrieve mappings to a selected ontology, with NCIT used in the experiments because it was recommended by the NCBO recommender. title: Relation Extraction with Matrix Factorization and Universal Schemas
domain: New York Times newswire text, Freebase facts, NER mentions linked to Freebase entities, and lexicalized dependency paths between co-sentential entity mentions.
research_problem: Relation extraction normally targets a fixed, finite schema and needs manually labeled text or an existing structured source with that schema. The paper seeks to populate a flexible universal schema, predict missing binary relation facts, generalize beyond explicit textual mentions, and jointly exploit textual surface patterns and Freebase relations.
methodology: The system constructs a sparse fact matrix whose rows are cross-document-resolved entity pairs and whose columns are both lexicalized dependency-path surface patterns and Freebase relations. It scores a relation–tuple cell with a logistic model. F factorizes relation and tuple embeddings; N sums directed relation-neighborhood weights for relations observed on the same tuple; E learns latent entity vectors and relation-slot vectors for selectional preferences. title: A Novel Cascade Binary Tagging Framework for Relational Triple Extraction
methodology_family: Joint entity-relation extraction (including joint triple extraction)
domain: A single unstructured natural-language sentence, represented as WordPiece subword tokens and encoded with BERT.
research_problem: Extract relational triples (subject, relation, object) from individual unstructured natural-language sentences for knowledge-graph construction, with particular emphasis on sentences containing overlapping triples: entity-pair overlap (EPO) and single-entity overlap (SEO). The paper argues that entity-pair relation classification suffers from severe negative-pair imbalance and ambiguity when an entity participates in several relations.
methodology: CasRel reformulates relation extraction as subject-conditioned object tagging rather than classifying a relation for an entity pair. Given a labelled sentence, its triple-level likelihood is decomposed into p(subject | sentence) and, for every relation, p(object | subject, sentence), including a null object for relations not holding for that subject. Execution is: (1) WordPiece-tokenize and encode one sentence with a 12-layer BERT encoder; (2) two sigmoid binary classifiers tag every token as a possible subject start and end; (3) pair starts with their nearest admissible ends to form subject spans; (4) represent each subject by the average of its start-to-end encoder vectors; (5) for that subject, run all relation-specific binary object start/end taggers in parallel, conditioned by adding the subject vector to each token representation; (6) pair object boundaries and emit every detected (subject, relation, object) triple. Training maximizes the summed log likelihood of subject, relation-object, and null-object tags using Adam.

entity_extraction: ["Entity and concept extraction"]
ontology_schema_use: No ontology or external KG schema is used to constrain decoding. The model assumes the fixed, predefined relation inventory of each dataset and creates one relation-specific object tagger per possible relation (24 relations for NYT; 246 for WebNLG).

title: CTI-Thinker: an LLM-driven system for CTI knowledge graph construction and attack reasoning
domain: Unstructured cyber threat intelligence text, including APT analysis reports, threat-event and vulnerability alerts, technical blogs, and cybersecurity consultancy material.
research_problem: The paper addresses the conversion of heterogeneous, fragmented, and largely unstructured cyber threat intelligence reports into semantically consistent knowledge graphs that support ATT&CK-aligned attack-chain reasoning. It targets limitations of prior systems including dependence on manual annotation, isolated entity or relation extraction, weak cross-paragraph context handling, polysemy and ambiguity, fragmented entity alignment, hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and limited tactical-level inference.
methodology: CTI-Thinker is a four-stage LLM-based pipeline. It collects and cleans multi-source CTI, segments documents into paragraphs and sentences, and uses expert-reviewed LLM-generated annotations. A KNN retriever selects semantically similar demonstrations for in-context prompting. A LoRA-adapted LLaMA-3-8B generates standardized entity-relation triples. A two-stage alignment module first groups entities and relations by semantic category using an LLM, then applies encoder embeddings and cosine similarity with a validation-tuned threshold to merge aliases and variants. The resulting graph and summaries are indexed for GraphRAG, which retrieves relevant nodes, neighboring subgraphs, ATT&CK knowledge, and STIX 2.1 information to generate evidence-oriented tactical reasoning and question-answering responses.

title: Entity linking for biomedical literature
domain: Unstructured full-text biomedical literature, plus an aggregated biomedical ontology knowledge base.
research_problem: Biomedical entity linking: identify prominent entity mentions in unstructured full-text biomedical literature and ground them in knowledge-base or ontology reference entities. The work addresses scarce labeled biomedical EL data and insufficient context for ambiguous mentions, with the intended downstream benefit of enriching literature and supporting biological-process modelling.
methodology: Execution pipeline: (1) aggregate 300 BioPortal biology ontologies into a knowledge-base graph whose vertices are classes, individuals, and properties and whose edges are ontology triples; (2) extract prominent mentions using a name tagger, regex-based mention joining, and shallow noun-phrase parsing; (3) retrieve candidates through a surface-form dictionary made from labels, names, synonyms, aliases, and symbols; (4) pre-rank candidates using EntropyRank, a recursive, PageRank-like salience score weighted by entropy of ontology relation properties, with partial surface matches penalized using Jaccard similarity; (5) build a document graph linking mentions by sentence- or paragraph-level co-occurrence; (6) collectively score each mention–candidate pair using candidate salience plus matches between the candidate's ontology neighbors and the mention's document-graph neighbors; and (7) select the highest-scoring candidate. Experiments set α=15 and β=8.

entity_extraction: ["Entity and concept extraction", "Entity resolution and linking"]
ontology_schema_use: The method is explicitly ontology-guided. It merges 300 BioPortal biology ontologies into a web of data with over 2 million entities and over 50 million factual statements. Ontology classes, properties, and individuals are candidate reference entities; ontology triples form the knowledge graph; labels, synonyms, aliases, and symbols populate the surface-form dictionary; relation-property entropy supplies edge weights; and ontology neighbor relations provide collective-disambiguation evidence.

title: Knowledge Base Population: Successful Approaches and Challenges
domain: Unstructured English newswire, web documents, and some transcribed spoken documents, together with entity queries and background documents.
research_problem: The paper analyzes how to discover and integrate facts about entities from large, heterogeneous newswire and web document collections into a knowledge base. It addresses Entity Linking and Slot Filling, including candidate generation and ranking, retrieval, relation/attribute extraction, answer combination, cross-document coreference, inference, redundancy and conflict handling, and the limitations of the 2010 KBP evaluation setting.
methodology: This is an analytical overview rather than a single newly proposed extractor. It synthesizes approaches used by 2010 KBP participants. Entity Linking is organized as query expansion, candidate generation, and candidate ranking using Wikipedia structure, document context, information retrieval, similarity, supervised classifiers, rules, or graph ranking. Slot Filling combines passage retrieval, IE or QA-style answer extraction, redundancy removal, answer validation, distant or weak supervision, bootstrapping, supervised classification, rules, and recursive cross-slot reasoning. The paper also evaluates system combination and identifies difficult cases requiring coreference and inference.

title: N-ary Relation Extraction for Simultaneous T-Box and A-Box Knowledge Base Augmentation
domain: Unstructured Italian Wikipedia article text in the soccer domain, extracted from Wikipedia markup; DBpedia is also queried for ontology classes/instances and existing assertions.
research_problem: Automatically enrich DBpedia from unstructured Wikipedia text by extracting meaningful, disambiguated factual assertions. The objective is to discover Frame-Semantic N-ary relations and produce RDF suitable for simultaneous A-Box fact population and candidate T-Box property augmentation, while avoiding deep parsing and costly expert annotation.
methodology: FACT EXTRACTOR first strips Wikipedia to raw text, tokenizes, lemmatizes, and POS-tags it with TreeTagger; ranks verb lexical units using TF-IDF dispersion; and maps selected verbs to a hand-built, Italian soccer Frame-Semantic repository (6 frames, 15 frame elements). It selects 5–25-word seeds, crowdsources bottom-up annotations, trains SVM FE and frame classifiers using token/lemma, context-window, predicted-role, entity-linking, and DBpedia gazetteer features, then normalizes numeric expressions using regex/transformation rules. Finally it represents each extracted frame as an RDF N-ary relation, adds type/provenance/confidence triples, and links entity mentions with The Wiki Machine to DBpedia URIs.

The system maps six frames and fifteen FEs in the use case, manually identifies mappings such as ACTIVITY→careerStation, AWARD→award, STATUS→playerStatus, and uses DBpedia classes in the entity-linking gazetteer.

research_problem: The paper seeks an effective and reliable way to construct a domain-specific military knowledge graph from heterogeneous, largely unstructured open-source intelligence, addressing ambiguity, limited data, difficult entity linking, knowledge redundancy, and the need to fuse newly extracted knowledge with existing knowledge bases.
methodology: The method is a sequential military Text-to-KG pipeline. Open-source military news and related semi-structured sources are collected, cleaned, and manually annotated. RoBERTa-wwm-ext encodes Chinese text; a BiLSTM-CRF performs BIO named-entity recognition; and a RoBERTa-wwm-ext plus fully connected softmax classifier predicts relations for entity pairs. Extracted knowledge is organized into ontology-compatible triples, matched with external knowledge bases, filtered into candidate entity pairs, aligned using longest-common-attribute similarity and a binary classifier, merged, stored in Neo4j, and visualized. A second fusion stage supports knowledge expansion and updating.

title: A Semantic Best-Effort Approach for Extracting Structured Discourse Graphs from Wikipedia
domain: Unstructured English natural-language text from Wikipedia articles.
research_problem: The paper addresses extraction of irregular, contextualized, semantically dependent, poorly structured, and ambiguous information from unstructured text into RDF-compatible structured discourse graphs. Its objective is to maximize text-semantic coverage and context capture under a pay-as-you-go quality perspective, accepting lower accuracy, schema consistency, and terminological normalization than conventional ontology- or database-oriented information extraction.
methodology: Graphia implements a sequential semantic-best-effort pipeline. It parses English Wikipedia sentences into Stanford PCFG syntactic C-Structures; resolves named entities with DBpedia Spotlight and a local TF/IDF DBpedia URI index; resolves personal, possessive, and reflexive coreferences using gender/number agreement and text-distance heuristics; maps annotated C-Structures to sentence-level triple trees using DFS syntactic transformation rules; detects explicit and implicit temporal references; and serializes the triple trees as an RDF-compatible graph with context URIs and local URIs for unresolved resources. The representation uses named and non-named entities, properties, quantifiers and generic operators, triple trees, reification, temporal context, coreference links, and resolved or normalized entities. The method prioritizes broad semantic representation and interpretability of graph fragments over completeness and strict normalization.

Named entities map to RDF instances, non-named entities map to classes that may also be referenced as instances through punning, and named entities may be linked to DBpedia URIs. The approach deliberately trades schema consistency and terminological normalization for context capture and wider coverage; unresolved resources receive local URIs.

title: Coarse-to-fine Knowledge Graph Domain Adaptation based on Distantly-supervised Iterative Training
domain: Unstructured English oncology-domain text from papers in 12 international journals, together with an existing biomedical KG for distant supervision.
research_problem: The paper addresses construction of a domain-specific oncology knowledge graph from large collections of raw or unlabeled biomedical text when manually annotated training data are scarce. It specifically adapts a coarse biomedical KG to oncology while recovering oncology-specific entities and relation triples absent from the source KG.
methodology: KGDA takes an existing coarse-domain KG K_c and an unlabeled target-domain corpus D, divides D into non-overlapping subsets, and alternates prediction, distant-corpus construction, and retraining. For the first subset, entity mentions are string-matched against K_c to create BIO-labelled NER data; relation instances are created from matched entity pairs, with NULL negatives sampled from unrelated pairs or out-of-domain words. Separate pretrained-language-model NER and RE classifiers are fine-tuned with cross-entropy. For later subsets, the current models predict entities and triples disjoint from K_c; high-confidence predictions are selected using probability and cumulative-frequency thresholds, added to the external knowledge bases, and used to create cumulative distant-supervision corpora for the next iteration. The final fine-domain KG combines overlapping triples with high-confidence target-domain triples. The method covers preprocessing, NER, entity typing through the source schema, relation/triple extraction, confidence filtering, and graph construction; separate coreference, entity linking, ontology discovery, and graph-validation modules are not reported.

title: Entity Linking with a Knowledge Base: Issues, Techniques, and Solutions
domain: English natural-language Web text, including unstructured documents, news articles, blogs, tweets, Web tables, Web lists, textual extractions, queries, and text associated with information-extraction outputs.
research_problem: The survey addresses how to map ambiguous and variably expressed named-entity mentions in English natural-language text to the correct entities in an existing knowledge base, including identifying mentions that have no corresponding knowledge-base record. The objective is to organize and analyze candidate generation, candidate ranking, unlinkable-mention prediction, applications, features, and evaluation.
methodology: This is a survey rather than a single trained system. It defines entity linking over an input text collection with preidentified named-entity mentions and a knowledge base containing entities, types, names, and relations. The surveyed pipeline first generates candidate entities using name dictionaries, local-document surface-form expansion, or search engines; ranks candidates using string, popularity, type, textual-context, semantic, topical-coherence, probabilistic, graph, information-retrieval, or supervised-learning evidence; and finally predicts NIL for mentions that are not linkable. The review also covers joint NER-linking, collective document or user-level linking, model combination, crowdsourcing, and domain-specific linking. Reported supervised approaches include binary classifiers, ranking SVMs, Ranking Perceptron, ListNet, probabilistic models, and graph-based collective inference; unsupervised approaches include vector-space and information-retrieval ranking.

title: Extensive Benchmark of Frugal Encoder–Decoder Language Models for Datatype Properties Extraction and RDF Knowledge Graph Generation
domain: English Wikipedia abstracts paired with a DBpedia entity URI; training labels are DBpedia graphs containing selected dbo:Person datatype properties.
research_problem: Determine how RDF output linearization affects fine-tuned frugal encoder-decoder models for extracting datatype-property facts from Wikipedia abstracts and directly generating RDF graphs for DBpedia dbo:Person resources. The paper specifically seeks the model/syntax trade-off that maximizes extraction quality and expressivity while minimizing cost.
methodology: The method treats restricted relation extraction as supervised sequence-to-sequence translation from a Wikipedia abstract plus the target DBpedia entity URI to a linearized RDF graph. Pipeline order: (1) obtain a DBpedia dump and matching Wikipedia abstracts; (2) select dbo:Person datatype triples; (3) retain graph descriptions valid against a maximal SHACL shape and retain only triples whose values occur in the paired abstract; (4) order triples with rdf:type first and URL-encode/clean URIs; (5) serialize each graph in 13 alternatives—list/tags and factorized versions, RDF/XML, N-Triples, Turtle, JSON-LD, Turtle Light variants, and Turtle Ultra Light—with vocabulary extensions for W3C syntaxes; (6) make cross-validation splits; (7) fine-tune BART, T5, CodeT5, FlanT5, and PileT5 base models using model-specific prompts; (8) parse generated output and measure RDF validity, SHACL validity, subject correctness, extraction quality, learning dynamics, training time, and CO2. Supplementary experiments test EBNF grammar-constrained decoding, CodeT5-based refinement, and robustness to reordered/masked/no-URI/no-instruction prompts. No entity linking, coreference resolution, or joint entity-relation extraction module is described; the supplied entity URI identifies the graph subject.

title: Importance sampling for unbiased on-demand evaluation of knowledge base population
domain: Large unstructured text document corpus (e.g., TAC KBP newswire documents)
research_problem: Traditional KBP evaluation relies on pooled predictions from existing systems; a new system that predicts a previously unseen (but correct) relation is penalized because it is missing from the pool, creating a systematic 'pooling bias' against new/innovative systems and discouraging progress in the field.
methodology: The paper proposes 'on-demand evaluation', which lazily constructs an evaluation dataset by annotating predictions from new KBP systems only when they are underrepresented in the current labeled pool. Using importance sampling, joint precision and recall estimators combine samples drawn independently from each system's predictions (weighted via mixing weights w_ij) with a sample of true instances (Y_0) to produce unbiased score estimates while minimizing crowdsourcing annotation cost, and an adaptive sampling scheme determines how many new labels are required for each newly submitted system.
pipeline_stages: ["entity identification/linking", "relation extraction", "provenance identification", "crowdsourced relation/entity labeling"]
entity_extraction: ["entity identification/linking", "crowdsourced relation/entity labeling"]
ontology_schema_use: Relations are triples (SUBJECT, PREDICATE, OBJECT, PROVENANCE) where PREDICATE belongs to a specified schema; the TAC KBP guidelines specify a total of 65 predicates (including inverses) such as per:title or org:founded_on.
evaluation_metrics: ["Precision", "Recall"]
main_results: ["Adaptive sample selection combined with joint estimation can reduce the number of labeled annotations required by an order of magnitude relative to a fixed sampling scheme (Figure 4e)"]
strengths: ["Eliminates pooling bias and reduces variance in KBP evaluation using importance-sampling based estimators (validated on TAC KBP 2015 data)", "Cost-effective: labeling relation instances from system predictions costs an order of magnitude less (~$0.18) than exhaustive annotation (~$1.60 per instance)", "Publicly available online evaluation service allowing researchers to obtain on-demand feedback without waiting for annual shared-task cycles"]
weaknesses: ["Determining the optimal mixing weights w_ij for the joint estimator is acknowledged to be a hard problem, so a heuristic approximation is used instead of an optimal solution", "Sampling from the true set of correct instances Y is inherently difficult since Y cannot be enumerated, requiring a proxy assumption (uniform distribution of relations across documents) that may not hold exactly"]
author_limitations: ["It is a hard problem to determine what the optimal mixing weights w_ij should be; a heuristic choice is used instead", "Sampling from the set of true instances Y is difficult because the elements of Y cannot even be enumerated, requiring an assumption that relations are identically distributed across documents", "Simply providing better evaluation scores is only part of the solution; better datasets are also necessary, and existing datasets likely still exhibit bias against novel systems"]
review_inferences: ["Adapting the on-demand/importance-sampling evaluation ideas to other hard-to-evaluate NLP tasks such as summarization or dialogue that have a generation component", "Further study of alternative sampling distributions p_i for selecting evaluation entities, as outlined for future analysis in the supplementary appendix"]
unresolved_problems: ["Existing large KBP datasets still rely on outputs of existing systems and are likely to exhibit the same pooling biases against novel systems discussed in the paper"]
reproducibility: The framework is implemented as a publicly available online evaluation service at https://kbpo.stanford.edu, where researchers can have their own KBP systems evaluated; data collected through the evaluation process will also be made publicly available through the website.

title: Large Language Models for Automatic Knowledge Graph Construction From Text Documents: a Materials Science Case Study
methodology_family: Zero-shot and few-shot LLM prompting (without task-specific model training)
domain: PDF text of materials-science scientific research articles, including article sections, figures and captions, and bibliography/references.
research_problem: How to use general LLMs to turn a materials-science research article into a valid, populated OWL ontology/knowledge-graph representation, and which model and prompting strategy yields the most complete and linked result. The study specifically tests whether prompt detail and staged generation mitigate the difficulty of creating logically consistent, domain-specific ontologies.
methodology: Contributions and workflow: (1) compares GPT-4, four Qwen variants, and DeepSeek-R1 on OWL generation from materials-science PDF articles; (2) designs and iteratively refines prompts from a general request (P1), through an explicit domain ontology schema (P2), to DeepSeek's staged creation/augmentation workflow (P3); (3) asks models to identify article metadata, authors, materials, processes, methods, properties, figures, results, and references; classify them as OWL classes/individuals; and emit RDF/XML OWL with object and data properties; (4) loads/parses outputs with Jena-Fuseki and Protégé, executes SPARQL count queries, and compares triples, classes, properties, individuals, and linkage factors. Author-reported conclusion: staged DeepSeek-R1 is the best current approach in this study, but remains a human-supervised assistant rather than an autonomous ontology generator.

P2 supplies classes and expected properties for article, abstract, author, material, research method, process, material property, structural component, and results/findings; models may add classes/properties. DeepSeek P3 explicitly constructs the class hierarchy before object properties, datatype properties, and named individuals.

title: Natural vs programming language in LLM knowledge graph construction
domain: Unstructured natural-language text from medical case reports, news articles, and scientific literature.
research_problem: The study addresses whether small, open-weight LLMs can perform RDF triple extraction for knowledge-graph construction as well as or better than larger closed-source models, and whether programming-language prompts improve structured extraction relative to natural-language prompts. It also examines the effects of chain-of-thought training and model size.
methodology: The system treats KGC as generative RDF triple extraction. For each dataset, the authors construct prompts in either natural language or Python-like code, optionally adding rationale lists that explicitly enumerate candidate entities and relations. Models receive three in-context examples and generate triples for a target sentence. The main experiments apply LoRA adapters to decoder attention and MLP modules while freezing the base model, using 200 training steps, batch size 8, learning rate 2×10^-4, and 42M trainable parameters for the 7–8B models. The study evaluates 175 model/settings combinations, including natural-language and code-pretrained models, instruction-tuned and completion models, model-size variants, no-fine-tuning controls, a 70B QLoRA condition, an ICL-example ablation, training-step analysis, attention visualizations, and LoRA-module ablations. The output is parsed/evaluated as exact RDF triples; no separate entity-recognition, linking, or graph-validation module is reported.

title: OneRel: Joint Entity and Relation Extraction with One Module in One Step
domain: Unstructured natural-language sentences
research_problem: The paper addresses joint extraction of head entities, relations, and tail entities from unstructured text. It targets cascading errors caused by serial multi-module methods and redundant or incorrectly assembled triples caused by separately recognizing entities and relations. The objective is to identify all triples with one module in one step by classifying token-pair/relation combinations jointly.
methodology: OneRel formulates joint extraction as fine-grained triple classification. For every ordered token pair and predefined relation, a scoring-based classifier predicts one of four tags: HB-TB, HB-TE, HE-TE, or -. The model uses BERT token representations, a nonlinear projection of token-pair representations, relation representations, dropout, and softmax classification. Rel-Spec Horns Tagging marks boundary-token combinations for paired head and tail entities. Decoding splices head and tail spans from the boundary tags and reconstructs triples. The score function computes all relation scores for a token pair in parallel. The execution pipeline is: tokenize a sentence; encode tokens with pretrained BERT; enumerate token-pair/relation combinations; score and classify them; obtain the sparse relation-specific tag matrix; decode entity spans and relations from HB-TB, HB-TE, and HE-TE tags; output triples.

ontology_schema_use: The model uses a predefined relation inventory supplied by each dataset; it does not discover an ontology or construct an ontology. The relation-specific matrix is an internal extraction representation, not an external KG schema.

title: Automated Construction and Growth of a Large Ontology
domain: Semi-structured Wikipedia XML/HTML markup (infoboxes, category pages, redirects, links, article text), WordNet, limited-scope HTML/text corpora, and arbitrary unstructured Web HTML documents; SOFIE can also process tables, categories, and note-form text.
research_problem: Automatically construct and continuously expand a domain-independent ontology containing individuals, a hierarchical class taxonomy, relations, and factual assertions, while minimizing human effort and maintaining high accuracy. The central Text-to-KG problem is turning Wikipedia and arbitrary natural-language/Web documents into canonical ontological facts that can be reconciled with an existing knowledge base.
methodology: Execution-order architecture: (1) construct YAGO from the September 2008 English Wikipedia XML dump and WordNet: parse Wikipedia pages; harvest infoboxes using a manually specified attribute-to-relation map with domain/range constraints; derive types and facts from category patterns; map category heads to WordNet synsets; resolve redirects, normalize values/names, deduplicate, and type-check candidates; export reified facts with witnesses. (2) LEILA preprocesses limited-scope text (encoding/format cleanup, sentence detection, date/number normalization, stemming), parses sentences with Link Grammar, optionally resolves third-person pronouns to the preceding sentence subject, induces positive and negative relation patterns from seed examples/counterexamples, generalizes them with adaptive kNN or SVM, and emits candidate binary relation pairs. (3) SOFIE adapts LEILA into a faster surface-pattern generator for arbitrary Web, Wikipedia, tables, categories, infoboxes, and note-like text; represents pattern occurrences and document-level word-in-context disambiguation priors as textual facts; creates hypotheses for entity senses, pattern-to-relation meanings, and canonical facts; grounds ontology/text rules; and selects a consistent, sparse set of true hypotheses through weighted MAX-SAT using FMS* plus dominating-unit-clause propagation. Accepted facts and optionally learned pattern meanings are added to YAGO for later runs.

title: A Method for Traditional Chinese Medicine Knowledge Graph Dynamic Construction
domain: Public Traditional Chinese Medicine textual data collected from several fixed websites in response to user search keywords.
research_problem: Existing TCM knowledge graphs are generally constructed once from currently available data and therefore cannot continuously incorporate multi-source information in response to users' search needs. The paper aims to construct a TCM knowledge graph that grows dynamically when a user's query is not covered by the existing graph.
methodology: The system is a query-triggered pipeline. For each keyword in a user search, it collects related public data from several fixed websites and keeps sentences satisfying downstream processing requirements. BERT-CRF converts each sentence into BIO-labelled entity spans for six TCM-specific entity types: color, form, smell, taste, cause, and symptom. A Bootstrapping procedure begins with expert-defined semantic patterns and seed entity pairs, removes entities, participles, and stop words to identify relation-trigger candidates, expands the semantic-pattern and trigger-word sets, and uses expert review to finalize trigger words. It extracts cause–symptom triples when a finalized trigger occurs between an entity pair. The newly constructed graph is merged with the existing graph by replacing an entity in the new graph with an existing entity when they are considered the same; otherwise the entity is added, followed by adding new relations and facts. The updated graph is then shown to the user. No separate mechanism is reported for coreference resolution, general entity linking, entity typing beyond the six predefined types, ontology discovery, or graph validation beyond the merge/refinement rule.

title: Confidence Estimation for Knowledge Base Population
domain: Newswire and web-document corpus, plus person and organization entity queries and an initial KB derived from Wikipedia infoboxes.
research_problem: The paper addresses unreliable intermediate outputs from multi-pipeline Knowledge Base Population (KBP) slot filling. It estimates each extracted slot fill's probability of correctness so heterogeneous pipeline outputs can be comparably re-ranked, filtered, and aggregated into more accurate KB population results.
methodology: Execution order: (1) retrieve documents matching a person or organization query name, optionally using query expansion; (2) preprocess retrieved text with POS tagging, name tagging, and coreference resolution; (3) run six parallel slot-filling pipelines—two hand-coded-pattern systems, two semi-automatically bootstrapped pattern systems, one name-coreference system, and one distant-supervision system—to produce intermediate query-slot-response fills; (4) compute a MaxEnt correctness probability for every intermediate response from response, pipeline, local-sentence, and global corpus features; (5) remove low-confidence responses and perform weighted response voting, summing supporting probabilities for each response entity; (6) select the highest-weight response for single-valued slots and all non-redundant fills for list-valued slots, then optionally suppress final fills below a final-confidence threshold. The confidence layer is trained/evaluated using ten-fold cross-validation over prior TAC KBP slot-filling evaluation data.

title: Distantly supervised Web relation extraction for knowledge base population
domain: Unstructured text extracted from HTML Web pages, retrieved by Google Search API and annotated using Freebase entity lexicalisations.
research_problem: Populate large cross-domain knowledge bases from unstructured heterogeneous Web text without manual domain adaptation. The authors target shortcomings of prior distant supervision for Web extraction: unrecognised nonstandard entities, sentence-boundary restrictions that cause sparsity, ambiguous object lexicalisations that create noisy labels, and lack of integration across redundant Web documents.
methodology: Execution pipeline: (1) select seven Freebase classes and five to seven properties each; retrieve entities and Web pages with Google Search queries; (2) extract HTML text with Jsoup, then use Stanford CoreNLP for sentence splitting, tokenisation, POS tagging, time normalisation, NER, and optionally coreference; (3) add a custom boundary-only entity recogniser using noun/capitalised-word sequences and quoted strings; (4) align subject/object lexicalisations from Freebase to automatically label positive and negative sentence candidates; (5) filter ambiguous training seeds with Stop, Unam, Stat, and StatRes; (6) extract lexical, POS, context, order, and NE features; (7) train one multiclass logistic-regression classifier per class to predict a property or NONE for each relation mention; (8) support a relaxed paragraph setting with Stanford or gazetteer-based coreference; and (9) aggregate mention predictions using Comb, Aggr, Limit, and MultiLab strategies to produce KB relations.

entity_extraction: ["Entity and concept extraction", "Entity typing"]
ontology_schema_use: The Freebase knowledge base supplies the schema-constrained classes, properties, subject/object entities, and their lexicalisations. Only triples already in Freebase are used for distant labels; extraction is performed per selected class and predicts its applicable properties.

title: Effective Modeling of Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Joint Entity and Relation Extraction
domain: Tokenized natural-language sentences.
research_problem: The paper addresses joint extraction of relation tuples from sentences when tuples may share one or both entities, entities may overlap, and entity names may contain multiple tokens. It aims to avoid the limitations of pipeline systems and earlier joint or encoder-decoder models that cannot reliably extract overlapping tuples or full entity spans.
methodology: The method has two encoder-decoder variants. WordDecoding encodes the input with word and character-CNN embeddings followed by a Bi-LSTM, then generates a serialized target sequence containing entity1, entity2, relation, and separator tokens one word at a time. A masking-based softmax restricts generated words to source tokens, relation tokens, separators, UNK, and EOS; duplicate and invalid tuples are removed after decoding. PtrNetDecoding removes entity and separator tokens from the decoder vocabulary and represents each tuple by two entity start/end spans plus a relation. Its decoder uses an LSTM, two pointer networks for entity spans, and a relation-classification network, generating one complete tuple per step. Attention variants and a masking/copy mechanism are evaluated.
pipeline_stages: ["Entity and concept extraction", "Relation and triple extraction"]
entity_extraction: ["Entity and concept extraction"]
ontology_schema_use: The method uses a predefined relation set R rather than discovering an ontology. The word-decoder vocabulary contains source tokens, relation names, separator tokens, SOS, EOS, and UNK; the pointer decoder uses relation embeddings for the predefined relations and EOS. The NYT29 and NYT24 datasets contain 29 and 24 relation types respectively.
datasets: ["NYT29: 63,306 training and 4,006 test sentences; 78,973 training and 5,859 test tuples; 29 relations", "NYT24: 56,196 training and 5,000 test sentences; 88,366 training and 8,120 test tuples; 24 relations", "For both datasets, 10% of the original training data is used for validation and the remaining 90% for training"]

strengths: ["The method jointly extracts entities and relations, directly addressing interaction among multiple tuples.", "The tuple representations support overlapping entities and full multi-token entity names.", "The masking-based copy mechanism prevents ordinary generated entity tokens from coming from outside the source sentence while retaining an UNK fallback.", "PNDec reduces decoding steps and resource use by extracting a complete tuple per step.", "Review-level inference: the method produces structured relation tuples that can serve as inputs to downstream knowledge-graph construction, but the paper does not evaluate graph construction itself."]

title: Entity Disambiguation for Knowledge Base Population
domain: An entity-linking query: a textual entity mention in a document, possibly supplied by a named-entity recognizer, plus a Wikipedia-derived knowledge base whose entries include titles, article text, attributes, and types.
research_problem: Entity linking for knowledge-base population: map a textual person, organization, or geo-political-entity mention in a document to its canonical KB/Wikipedia entry, or return NIL when no corresponding KB entry exists. The method targets name variants, mention ambiguity, and KB absence, which otherwise impede integrating extracted facts into an existing KB.
methodology: Execution pipeline: (1) receive an entity-linking query consisting of a textual mention and its document; a named-entity recognizer may identify the mention. (2) Retrieve a compact candidate set from a Wikipedia-derived KB using exact/containment/acronym/alias and string-similarity title matches; an indexed implementation precomputes non-string filters and skip-bigram Dice features and serves the KB concurrently. (3) For each query–candidate pair, build roughly 200 atomic features, expanded to 26,569 conjunction features: normalized/exact and approximate name matching, acronym and alias evidence, trained finite-state-transducer name similarity, Wikipedia graph/category and Google popularity evidence, document–KB text similarity, KB facts, and predicted/KB entity types. SERIF supplies named and nominal coreferent mentions used as document features. (4) Train a linear maximum-margin SVMrank so the gold candidate outranks incorrect candidates. (5) Add NIL as a rankable candidate and score NIL-specific aggregate and match/context features; output the highest-ranked KB entry or NIL. No LLM, prompting, transformer, generative graph extraction, relation extraction output, or task-specific fine-tuning is reported.
pipeline_stages: ["Entity typing", "Coreference resolution", "Entity resolution and linking"]
entity_extraction: ["Entity typing", "Entity resolution and linking"]
ontology_schema_use: The system does not require an ontology or schema for its core candidate selection and ranking. Its evaluated KB is derived from English Wikipedia pages containing infoboxes, whose article text and attributes provide candidate evidence and types. Optional Wikipedia-specific features include graph statistics, Wikitology category/taxonomy evidence, and Google results; Wikitology categories are used as ranking and NIL features rather than as output schema discovery.

title: Entity extraction: From unstructured text to DBpedia RDF triples
domain: Unstructured natural-language text from English Wikipedia articles after removal of WikiMarkup.
research_problem: The paper addresses the problem of extracting structured entity-relation information from the unstructured text of Wikipedia articles and integrating the extracted information with the DBpedia ontology and namespace. Its objective is to extend DBpedia beyond information already available in infoboxes and other structured or semi-structured article content.
methodology: The method is a seven-module pipeline executed in sequence: WikiMarkup filtering; Wikipedia-link extraction; Athena semantic parsing with semantic role labeling; Stanford CoreNLP coreference resolution; mention-to-entity linking using article links and Wikifier; information alignment and entity extraction; and ontology mapping from PropBank predicate-argument roles to DBpedia properties. Semantic-role arguments provide candidate subjects and objects, coreference chains propagate representative entity links across mentions and sentences, and extracted predicates are first represented in the PropBank namespace. The mapping component bootstraps PropBank-to-DBpedia property mappings from matching subject-object pairs in existing DBpedia triples, generalizing entities to DBpedia ontology classes. The resulting mapped triples are serialized as DBpedia RDF N-Triples. The method does not use joint neural extraction, prompting, or fine-tuning; its central mechanisms are linguistic analysis, rules, linking, and bootstrapped schema mapping.

relation_extraction: ["Relation and triple extraction: Athena semantic role labeling identifies PropBank predicates and arguments; binary relations are generated from n-ary predicate-argument structures.", "Graph construction: mapped subject-predicate-object records are serialized as DBpedia RDF N-Triples.", "Knowledge fusion and deduplication: extracted triples are compared with existing DBpedia triples and repeated or already-present triples are identified."]
ontology_schema_use: The system uses the PropBank roleset and predicate-argument schema during semantic parsing, then maps PropBank predicates and argument roles to the DBpedia property ontology. DBpedia URIs and ontology classes constrain entity linking and candidate selection; predicted links whose DBpedia class conflicts with the Stanford named-entity class are pruned. Mapping generalization uses 43 top-level DBpedia ontology classes, plus String, Date, and Number categories.

title: Knowledge Graphs Generation from Cultural Heritage Texts: Combining LLMs and Ontological Engineering for Scholarly Debates
domain: Raw English Wikipedia articles about Cultural Heritage historical forgeries, hoaxes, and authenticity controversies, stored as markup/text files, with extracted item metadata and selected contextual paragraphs passed between stages.
research_problem: The paper addresses the gap between rich, interpretative Cultural Heritage scholarly discourse in unstructured texts and sparse structured KGs. It aims to extract agents, competing authenticity claims, evidence, and alternative hypotheses while retaining provenance and multi-perspectival reasoning.
methodology: ATR4CH is a five-step iterative Text-to-RDF methodology: (I) analyse corpus, target ontology, competency questions, and core ontological patterns; (II) create and validate a minimal working annotation schema and annotation-to-RDF mapping on a pilot corpus; (III) design a modular extraction architecture around that schema; (IV) test end-to-end, refine the production KG annotation model and mappings; (V) extract a held-out test set and perform technical, semantic, competency-based, and expert evaluation. Its case-study implementation is a six-stage sequential pipeline: LLM metadata extraction; GliNER entity detection plus few-shot LLM cognizer classification/coreferences; rule-based Wikidata entity linking; LLM opinion extraction/classification; LLM evidence-feature-evaluation extraction; and LLM hypothesis extraction. JSON-schema outputs are mapped to RDF-star/SEBI graphs.

title: Laying the Groundwork for Knowledge Base Population: Nine Years of Linguistic Resources for TAC KBP
domain: Unstructured multilingual text in English, Chinese, and Spanish, primarily formal newswire and informal web text including blogs and discussion forums.
research_problem: The paper documents how to create, maintain, and assess multilingual linguistic resources for TAC KBP systems that extract entities, relations, events, sentiments, and associated information from unstructured text to populate existing or emergent knowledge bases. It addresses the increasing complexity of KBP evaluation, including multilinguality, multiple genres, cross-document and cross-lingual clustering, event representation, and end-to-end Cold Start graph construction.
methodology: The work is a longitudinal resource-construction and evaluation methodology rather than a single extraction model. LDC selects multilingual newswire, blogs, and discussion-forum documents; constructs reference knowledge bases; defines task-specific schemas and query pools; produces labeled training and evaluation annotations; creates human responses or gold standards; and assesses system submissions. The paper traces seven primary tracks: Entity Linking, Entity Discovery & Linking, Slot Filling and its variants, Event Argument Linking, Event Nugget, Belief and Sentiment, and Cold Start. The pipeline evolves from isolated entity or slot tasks toward integrated multilingual end-to-end KB construction with cross-document clustering and event/sentiment information.

ontology_schema_use: The resources use predefined KBP entity types and slot schemas, event type/subtype and argument-role taxonomies, ERE annotations, belief and sentiment labels, and knowledge-base representations. The initial reference KB contains person, organization, and geopolitical-entity nodes with attributes derived from Wikipedia infoboxes; later evaluations use BaseKB represented in RDF. ERE specifies taxonomies for entities, relations, events, and attributes.

title: Multi-Task Identification of Entities, Relations, and Coreference for Scientific Knowledge Graph Construction
domain: Unstructured natural-language scientific article abstracts (AI conference/workshop proceedings); the model input is a document represented as a sequence of words.
research_problem: Scientific literature needs to be organized into structured knowledge bases, but scientific entity/relation extraction is costly and existing information-extraction pipelines suffer cascading errors and primarily model within-sentence relations. The objective is to jointly identify scientific entities, typed relations, and coreference clusters so cross-sentence relations can contribute to a denser scientific knowledge graph.
methodology: SciIE enumerates candidate within-sentence spans up to a maximum width, encodes the document with a one-layer BiLSTM, and constructs each span vector from its endpoint representations, attention-based soft headword, and span-width embedding. Task-specific FFNNs score entity labels, relation mentions, coreference mentions, relation pairs, and coreference pairs while sharing span representations. It jointly optimizes weighted entity, relation, and marginalized coreference losses. Beam pruning retains relation and coreference candidate spans, then the model outputs entity types, within-sentence typed relations, and antecedent links. For graph construction, it processes each abstract, uses coreference clusters to replace generic mentions and selects the longest cluster string, normalizes acronyms/plurals, retains frequent entities as nodes, merges substring variants, and assigns each entity-pair edge its most frequent relation type across the corpus.

These types define graph node/edge semantics.

title: OPIEC: An Open Information Extraction Corpus
domain: Full unstructured English Wikipedia article text, with retained internal Wikipedia hyperlinks; the appendix evaluation additionally uses sentences from the New York Times corpus.
research_problem: The work addresses the lack of a very large, richly annotated open-information-extraction resource for automated knowledge-base construction. It constructs and characterizes a Wikipedia-derived corpus, including cleaner and entity-linked subsets, and tests how its open facts overlap with DBpedia and YAGO. Author contributions: (1) release OPIEC and the OPIEC-Clean and OPIEC-Linked subcorpora; (2) build a scalable extraction pipeline with provenance, confidence, syntactic, factuality, spatial, and temporal metadata; (3) extend MinIE to MinIE-SpaTe; (4) profile corpus quality and analyze alignment/complementarity with DBpedia and YAGO; and (5) release construction code and derived relation-frequency resources.
methodology: Execution-order architecture: (1) use a modified WikiExtractor on the 21 June 2017 English Wikipedia dump to produce plain text while preserving internal links as span-to-target annotations, and add a self-link for an article's first exact title mention; (2) run Stanford CoreNLP 3.8.0 for tokenization, sentence splitting, POS tagging, lemmatization, NER, temporal tagging, and dependency parsing; (3) run dependency/clause-based MinIE, based on ClausIE, to generate compact subject–relation–object triples; (4) extend it as MinIE-SpaTe, which transfers polarity, modality, attribution, quantities, and detected temporal/spatial context into annotations, using SUTime, NER, and dependency rules; (5) remove a recurring erroneous NER-type-mismatched “be” pattern, estimate extraction confidence with logistic regression, and repair split Wikipedia links; (6) retain all outputs as OPIEC, then filter clean entity/concept triples for OPIEC-Clean and doubly Wikipedia-linked triples for OPIEC-Linked; and (7) profile corpus characteristics and compare linked facts against DBpedia and YAGO using distant supervision. The method is a corpus-construction and analysis pipeline, rather than a trained end-to-end KG generator.

Wikipedia page links provide golden entity disambiguation where present; OPIEC-Linked retains triples whose two arguments are linked. DBpedia and YAGO are used after extraction for distant-supervision alignment and comparative profiling, not as an extraction schema. Time is represented in TIMEX3 format.

title: A Holy Quran Ontology Construction with Semi-Automatic Population
domain: Unstructured natural-language religious texts: the Holy Quran, Sahih Al-Bukhari, and Sahih Muslim Hadith collections.
research_problem: Manual ontology population is time-consuming, while existing Quran ontologies do not contain all named-entity instances. The paper addresses construction of a named-entity ontology for the Holy Quran and semi-automatic discovery and population of additional instances using Quranic text and Sahih Al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim Hadith collections.
methodology: The authors first define the ontology domain and scope, reuse selected concepts from the Quran Corpus ontology, identify terms, build a hierarchical class taxonomy, define attributes and values, and then populate the ontology. Initial confident instances seed an iterative semi-automatic process. The system finds their occurrences in the Quran and two Hadith collections, extracts surrounding n-word contexts, ranks contexts using a TF-IDF-derived frequency scheme, searches for text segments matching retained contexts, treats matches as candidate named-entity instances, and sends candidates to an Islamic-knowledge expert for validation. Validated instances are added to the seed set and the process repeats. The ontology is implemented in Protégé 2000 and includes classes, subclasses, individuals, binary object properties, and class-equivalence constructs. The figures show the UML/class structure, class hierarchy, individuals, object properties, OWL equivalent-class representation, and OntoGraf visualizations.

title: A hybrid approach for extracting semantic relations from texts
domain: English electronic newsletter text from the Knowledge Media Institute (KMi), containing news about research-group members, projects, publications, events, and awards.
research_problem: Automatically identify semantic relations between pairs of known or new entities in raw text and convert them into semantic annotations; relations may already exist in the knowledge base, be permitted by the domain ontology, or be previously unpredicted. The stated applications are semantic-Web metadata enrichment, ontology population, and ontology learning.
methodology: Execution order: (1) GATE-based tokenization, sentence splitting, POS tagging, morphological analysis, VP chunking, lemmatization, and JAPE grammar identify shallow linguistic triples; Minipar complements these with functional/dependency relations and both are normalized as <noun phrase, verbal expression, noun phrase>. (2) RSS attempts exact and string-similarity entity-to-KB-instance mappings, preferring a substring match when multiple candidates remain; it maps verbs to KB/ontology relations using exact matching, string similarity, an Aqualog-derived mapping lexicon, and WordNet synonyms. (3) For unmapped/new terms, ESpotter++ assigns ontology classes; RSS then tests possible ontology relations between classes. (4) A unique compatible relation yields a semantic annotation and adds a generalized class-relation-class pattern. (5) Multiple compatible relations invoke SenseLearner WSD; no compatible relation invokes an unsupervised WordNet-similarity pattern classifier seeded by user-derived and manually defined patterns. Newly accepted patterns are added to the pattern repository. Review-level inference: the paper describes a modular, cascaded decision procedure rather than a jointly trained extractor.

title: A Survey on Generative Knowledge Graph Construction
domain: The surveyed KGC problem uses unstructured or semi-structured data sources, especially natural-language text/sentences/documents; the general formulation also permits webpages, tables, and multimodal content.
research_problem: The paper addresses how generative methods can automate knowledge graph construction from unstructured or semi-structured sources and overcome limitations of discriminative pipeline approaches, especially error propagation and limited cross-domain generalization. Its objective is to survey the evolution from Seq2Seq generation to LLM-driven full-process construction and compare their mechanisms, applications, benefits, limitations, and future directions.
methodology: This is a narrative survey, not a newly evaluated KGC model. It frames KGC as mapping raw data and background knowledge to a graph, then classifies the literature into discriminative and generative paradigms. For generative extraction, input text x is mapped autoregressively to a linearized target sequence y of triples/structures; pretrained Seq2Seq models such as MASS, T5, and BART can be fine-tuned with cross-entropy. It reviews: (1) copy-based generation, where a decoder copies subject/object spans from input while selecting relation labels, with reinforcement learning for triple order and Top-k pruning for documents; (2) structure-linearization, which serializes events/triples and can constrain decoding with event schemas; and (3) label-augmented generation, which inserts explicit entity/type labels in natural-language-like output. For LLM-era KGC, the surveyed execution patterns include top-down ontology assistance (natural-language requirements to formal ontology), bottom-up schema induction (open extraction, clustering, definition, and canonicalization), schema-guided or schema-free extraction, and schema-/instance-level fusion through alignment, disambiguation, conflict resolution, and verification. Review-level inference: because this paper synthesizes methods rather than implementing one, descriptions of architecture, prompts, training, and pipelines are literature-level categories, not a single reproducible workflow authored and tested by Zhao and Huang.

entity_extraction: ["Entity and concept extraction", "Entity typing", "Entity resolution and linking"]
ontology_schema_use: The survey treats background knowledge, rules, schemas, type hierarchies, and domain ontologies as constraints on the semantic space of a KG. It reviews top-down LLM-assisted ontology modelling from natural-language requirements into formal ontology; bottom-up schema induction through open extraction and clustering; ontology-guided RDF triple extraction; dynamic/evolving schemas; and schema-level alignment/canonicalization during fusion. Schema use is therefore a major reviewed component, not an ontology implemented by this survey.

title: Alzheimer’s Disease Knowledge Graph Enhances Knowledge Discovery and Disease Prediction
methodology_family: Supervised information extraction (joint named entity recognition and relation classification) for knowledge graph construction
domain: Biomedical literature text (PubMed abstracts related to Alzheimer's disease)
research_problem: Alzheimer's disease research literature is vast and fragmented, making it difficult to synthesize relationships among AD, genes, variants, chemicals, drugs, and other diseases; the paper addresses the need to systematically extract and organize this information into a structured, AD-specific knowledge graph to support drug repurposing, biomarker discovery, and disease prediction.
methodology: The authors annotate 800 PubMed abstracts (ADERC corpus) with BERN pre-labeling and BRAT manual annotation, and train a joint SpERT model with SciBERT embeddings for simultaneous entity recognition and relation classification. The trained model is applied to ~169,630 unannotated abstracts retrieved from PubMed to extract entity mentions and relation triplets. Entity linking constructs nodes and edges of the ADKG, which is further fused with external knowledge graphs (DisGeNET, HPO, DrugBank, PharmGKB, OMIM, STRING). Knowledge graph embedding models (TransE, TransH, TransR, ComplEx, ConvKB) are trained on ADKG for link prediction.

Entities are further linked to reference biomedical databases/ontologies including NCBI Gene, UniProt, ChEBI, DrugBank, HPO, Disease Ontology, ClinVar, and MeSH, and the ADKG is fused with external KGs (DisGeNET, PharmGKB, OMIM, STRING).

title: Bootstrapped Self Training for Knowledge Base Population.
domain: Unstructured textual sentences from the KBP source corpora, enriched with POS tags, lemmas, named-entity tags, dependency parses, entity mentions, and canonical entity links.
research_problem: The paper addresses relation extraction for knowledge-base population when manually supervised training data is scarce. It seeks to combine the high precision but low recall of hand-written patterns with the broader generalization of learned models, while controlling semantic drift and the precision loss caused by noisy or assumed-negative training examples.
methodology: The system starts with manually developed high-precision Tokensregex and Semgrex relation patterns, supplemented by Stanford OpenIE. Their predictions over the large unlabeled source corpus become positive training examples. A traditional L1-regularized logistic-regression extractor and a bidirectional LSTM sentence classifier are trained using these examples, supervised data, assumed negatives, and hand annotations. In subsequent self-training, predictions from the learned extractors are removed from the negative pool; for the submitted conservative version, positives remain the pattern outputs while negatives are regenerated. Six extractors—patterns, OpenIE, website, alternate names, supervised logistic regression, and neural LSTM—are optionally combined by a classifier using extractor-agreement and relation features. Predictions are stored and processed in a relational database before consistency/inference for slot filling or direct submission for the KB track.

ontology_schema_use: The extractors map OpenIE and other relation predictions into the KBP relation schema. Candidate relation mentions are type-checked using subject and object named-entity tags, and the system uses canonical entity links represented by Wikipedia titles or canonical surface forms. The paper does not describe a separately formalized ontology or schema-discovery procedure.

title: Construction of a knowledge graph for framework material enabled by large language models and its application
methodology_family: Zero-shot and few-shot LLM prompting (without task-specific model training)
domain: Web of Science bibliographic records: unstructured academic-paper abstracts for MOF, COF, and HOF literature, supplemented with structured publication metadata including DOI, authors, publication date, journal, and title.
research_problem: Framework-material research is dispersed across a very large, fragmented literature, while no comprehensive FM knowledge graph had been constructed. Manual conversion of unstructured literature into connected domain knowledge is labor-intensive; the study aims to automate construction of a KG covering MOFs, COFs, and HOFs and use it for retrieval, mining, and more accurate, source-grounded LLM question answering.
methodology: The paper presents KG-FM, a high-throughput Text-to-KG pipeline and a KG-augmented QA application. Execution order: (1) retrieve Web of Science records on MOF, COF, and HOF before 8 May 2024 and export abstracts plus bibliographic metadata as TXT; (2) prompt Qwen2-72B-Instruct to transform each abstract into structured JSON nodes and logical relations, with prompts defining tasks and output format; (3) manually inspect 100 LLM outputs; (4) convert JSON to Cypher and import it, along with title/DOI metadata and manually defined publication relations, into Neo4j 5.12.0; (5) query the graph directly or use a three-step RAG-style application that generates Cypher from a question, executes it over Neo4j, and formulates an answer from retrieved KG data. The study's central contributions are the large KG-FM resource, prompt-based abstract-to-JSON extraction, Neo4j graph construction, and evaluation/demonstration of KG-supported LLM retrieval and chain-of-thought material-screening reasoning.

title: DBpedia Spotlight: Shedding Light on the Web of Documents
domain: Unstructured natural-language text fragments, with DBpedia/Wikipedia-derived lexical and contextual data used to construct the annotation index.
research_problem: Automatically find natural-language mentions of DBpedia resources and disambiguate ambiguous surface forms to the correct DBpedia URI, so unstructured documents can be linked to the Web of Data. The system targets a broad set of DBpedia entity types and lets users trade annotation coverage against error tolerance.
methodology: Execution pipeline: (1) build a DBpedia lexicalization lexicon from DBpedia labels, redirects, disambiguation pages, and Wikipedia wikilinks; tokenize, remove stopwords, and stem wikilink-context paragraphs, then index resource occurrence contexts in Lucene; (2) spot longest case-insensitive lexicon matches with LingPipe/Aho-Corasick, optionally excluding spots consisting only of selected parts of speech; (3) retrieve DBpedia candidate resources for each surface form from the lexicalization dataset, retaining minimal pre-filtering; (4) represent each resource by aggregated Wikipedia mention contexts in a TF×ICF vector-space model and rank candidates by cosine similarity to the mention paragraph; (5) optionally combine the contextual score with the surface-form prior using linear-regression-derived weights; (6) post-filter/configure annotations by DBpedia class hierarchy or SPARQL-selected resource set, support/prominence, topical pertinence, contextual ambiguity, and confidence; (7) return linked annotations through a Web application or REST/SOAP service in HTML, XML, JSON, or XHTML+RDFa.
pipeline_stages: ["Text preprocessing", "Entity and concept extraction", "Entity resolution and linking", "Graph construction"]
entity_extraction: ["Entity and concept extraction", "Entity resolution and linking"]
ontology_schema_use: DBpedia is both the target knowledge base and a schema constraint: users may annotate only instances of specified DBpedia ontology classes (including subclasses), or use arbitrary SPARQL queries over DBpedia to define eligible resources. The lexicalization dataset is encoded in RDF with Lexvo labels and named-graph association scores.

title: DocOIE: A Document-level Context-Aware Dataset for OpenIE
domain: Unstructured natural-language patent text
research_problem: The paper addresses the lack of document-level context in existing sentence-level OpenIE systems and datasets. Without surrounding sentences, OpenIE may misinterpret part-of-speech and syntactic ambiguities, miss contextual information, or produce incorrect tuple boundaries. The objective is to create a context-aware benchmark and model that use surrounding document sentences to improve relational tuple extraction.
methodology: DocIE treats a document as a source sentence plus a symmetric window of surrounding context sentences. It concatenates source and context representations with trainable word and segment embeddings, uses bottom BERT blocks to model semantic interactions, keeps only the source representation, and applies additional top transformer blocks. A CopyAttention-style encoder-decoder then generates variable-length relational tuples, using a copying mechanism because tuple arguments and relations are usually input sub-spans. The training data are pseudo-labeled by traditional OpenIE systems selected on the expert-annotated DocOIE evaluation set.

ontology_schema_use: No domain ontology or fixed relation schema is used. The task is open-domain extraction of relational tuples represented as subject, relation, and object.

title: Extract, Define, Canonicalize: An LLM-based Framework for Knowledge Graph Construction
methodology_family: Zero-shot and few-shot LLM prompting (without task-specific base-model training)
domain: Unstructured natural-language text, with an optional predefined relation schema for target alignment; EDC+R additionally uses previously extracted triples and retrieved relation definitions as prompting hints.
research_problem: Automated knowledge graph construction from natural-language text, focused on relational triplet extraction and canonicalization. Existing prompt-based LLM KGC methods require target-schema information in the prompt, which does not scale to large schemas and is unsuitable when no fixed schema exists; open extraction also leaves redundant and ambiguous relation phrases.
methodology: EDC executes in order: (1) an LLM uses few-shot open information extraction to emit [subject, relation, object] triples without including a schema; (2) the LLM writes contextual natural-language definitions for extracted relation/schema components; (3) a sentence-transformer similarity search retrieves candidate relation components and the LLM verifies whether a proposed replacement is semantically valid. With a supplied target schema, non-alignable components and their triples are excluded; without one, non-alignable components are added to an initially empty canonical schema. Optional EDC+R performs another extraction pass using a hint containing prior extracted entities/relations plus top retrieved schema relations. Its fine-tuned E5-Mistral schema retriever maps text and defined relations into a relevance-oriented vector space. Contributions detailed: EDC supports both large predefined schemas and schema induction; the trained Schema Retriever improves refinement; experiments compare EDC/EDC+R against trained and canonicalization baselines across target-alignment and self-canonicalization settings.
pipeline_stages: ["Entity and concept extraction (entities in subject/object triple positions; optional candidate-entity extraction)", "Relation and triple extraction", "Ontology or schema discovery (self-generated canonical relation schema)", "Graph construction (open and canonicalized triplet KG)", "Knowledge fusion and deduplication (relation/schema canonicalization)", "Graph validation and correction (LLM verification of candidate schema substitutions; refinement)"]
entity_extraction: ["Entity and concept extraction (entities in subject/object triple positions; optional candidate-entity extraction)"]
relation_extraction: ["Entity and concept extraction (entities in subject/object triple positions; optional candidate-entity extraction)", "Relation and triple extraction", "Ontology or schema discovery (self-generated canonical relation schema)", "Graph construction (open and canonicalized triplet KG)", "Knowledge fusion and deduplication (relation/schema canonicalization)"]
ontology_schema_use: Schema is central and may be either externally supplied or induced. EDC defines each extracted relation in natural language, embeds definitions, retrieves nearest candidate schema components, and asks the LLM to validate replacement. In target alignment, triples must conform to the target schema and rejected mappings are excluded. In self-canonicalization, the system begins with an empty canonical schema and adds components when no valid equivalent exists; this is schema canonicalization, not ontology discovery in the formal ontology-engineering sense.
